oe.title: Sources of error in the back titration and checking accuracy
points: Limestone contains impurities that may also react with HCl (e.g. MgCO_3), overestimating CaCO_3; inert impurities are what's being measured.
Incomplete reaction of CaCO_3 (lumps, not enough time/heat) leaves CaCO_3 unreacted, underestimating it. Grind to a powder, warm, and let the CO_2 escape fully.
Loss of solution by spray/effervescence or transfer losses: transfer quantitatively with rinsings into the volumetric flask.
Dissolved CO_2 forms carbonic acid, which reacts with NaOH, so boil to remove CO_2 before titrating.
Apparatus/technique: weighing errors (weigh by difference), burette/pipette reading errors, parallax, air bubbles; NaOH not standardised (it absorbs CO_2).
Indicator choice/end point judgement (e.g. phenolphthalein); use concordant titres (within 0.1 cm^3).
Check accuracy: a control with pure calcium carbonate of known mass (should give ~100%), repeats, standardised solutions, or an independent method (gravimetric).
equations: CaCO_3 + 2HCl → CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2;   HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H_2O
n(HCl reacted) = n(HCl added) − n(HCl in excess, from titre × 4 for the 100 cm^3 flask); n(CaCO_3) = ½ n(HCl reacted)
% CaCO_3 = (n × 100.1 g mol^−1 / mass of limestone) × 100
diagrams: Flow diagram of the back titration steps.
Labelled titration set-up and volumetric flask.

oe.title: Mixtures from addition reactions and how to isolate the products
points: Unsymmetrical alkenes + HX/H_2O give two structural isomers. Markovnikov: the major product comes via the more stable (more substituted) carbocation, e.g. propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane (major) + 1-bromopropane (minor).
Addition at a C=C can create a chiral centre. The planar carbocation is attacked from either side, giving a racemic mixture (no net optical rotation).
Adding to dienes/alkynes: partial addition to an alkyne gives an alkene, which can be cis or trans (geometric isomers); further addition gives saturated products.
Halogen addition via a cyclic halonium ion gives anti addition (e.g. trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane).

Isolation: fractional distillation (structural isomers have different b.p. due to different intermolecular forces), chromatography (TLC/column/GC, different R_f), recrystallisation for solids, solvent extraction (separating funnel).
Enantiomers have identical physical properties, so they can't be separated by distillation; they need a chiral method (e.g. reacting with a single enantiomer or chiral chromatography).
Identify/confirm with IR, ^1H NMR, mass spectrometry, melting point and polarimetry.
diagrams: Curly-arrow mechanism showing primary vs secondary carbocations.
Fractional distillation apparatus or a TLC plate showing separated products.
